questions.q: State Joule's Law in words and write its mathematical formula with SI units for each quantity.
questions.a: Joule's Law: The heat produced in a conductor is directly proportional to the square of the current passing through it, its resistance, and the time for which current flows. Formula: H = I²Rt, where H is heat in joules (J), I is current in amperes (A), R is resistance in ohms (Ω), and t is time in seconds (s). A wrong answer (e.g., H = I R t or missing the square) reveals the student does not understand that heat depends on the square of current, a critical non-linear relationship.

questions.q: Why does the heat produced depend on the square of the current (I²) and not just on current (I)? Explain using the idea of electron collisions.
questions.a: Heat depends on I² because: (1) The number of electrons passing per second is proportional to I. (2) The kinetic energy each electron transfers per collision is also proportional to I (since drift velocity ∝ I). So total energy transferred per second (power) ∝ I × I = I². A wrong answer (e.g., "more current means more electrons so more heat") shows the student only sees the linear factor and misses that each electron also hits harder when current increases.

questions.q: An electric kettle has a heating coil of resistance 25 Ω. If a current of 8 A flows through it for 3 minutes, calculate the heat produced in joules.
questions.a:
Given: R = 25 Ω, I = 8 A, t = 3 min = 180 s.
Step 1: Identify formula H = I²Rt.
Step 2: Substitute: H = (8 A)² × 25 Ω × 180 s.
Step 3: Compute: 64 × 25 × 180 = 288,000 J.
Step 4: Unit check: A² × Ω × s = (C/s)² × (J·s/C²) × s = J. Correct.
Answer: 288,000 J (or 2.88 × 10⁵ J). A wrong answer (e.g., 36,000 J) suggests the student forgot to square the current or converted time incorrectly.

questions.q: Two identical resistors are connected (a) in series and (b) in parallel across the same battery. In which arrangement is more heat produced per minute? Explain using Joule's Law.
questions.a: Parallel arrangement produces more heat. Reason: For the same battery voltage, equivalent resistance in parallel is lower (R/2) than in series (2R). Current from battery is higher in parallel (I = V/(R/2) = 2V/R) than in series (I = V/(2R)). Heat per minute H = I²R_eq t. For series: H_s = (V/(2R))² × (2R) × t = (V²/2R)t. For parallel: H_p = (2V/R)² × (R/2) × t = (2V²/R)t. H_p is 4 times H_s. A wrong answer (e.g., "series because resistance is higher") shows the student thinks heat increases with resistance alone, ignoring that current changes more dramatically.

questions.q: A student calculates heat produced in a 10 Ω resistor with 2 A current for 5 minutes and gets 600 J. Evaluate if this answer is correct. If not, find the error.
questions.a: Correct calculation: H = I²Rt = (2)² × 10 × (5×60) = 4 × 10 × 300 = 12,000 J. The student's 600 J is wrong. Likely error: used time as 5 seconds instead of 5 minutes (4 × 10 × 5 = 200 J, not 600) or used H = I R t (2 × 10 × 300 = 6000 J). The exact 600 J suggests they did 2 × 10 × 30 = 600, maybe using 30 seconds? A wrong evaluation reveals the student cannot track units or spot the missing square on current.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a battery, a nichrome wire, and a thermometer to verify that heat produced is proportional to the square of the current. List the steps and what you would plot.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Set up a circuit with a battery, variable resistor (rheostat), ammeter, and a fixed length of nichrome wire immersed in a known mass of water in an insulated cup. (2) Adjust rheostat to get a current I₁, close switch for fixed time t, measure temperature rise Δθ₁. (3) Repeat for different currents I₂, I₃, etc., keeping t and water mass same. (4) Calculate heat H = mcΔθ for each. (5) Plot H vs I and H vs I². The H vs I² graph should be a straight line through origin. A poor answer (e.g., "measure heat for different currents" without controlling time, mass, or plotting I²) shows the student cannot design a controlled experiment to isolate the I² relationship.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The heating effect of electric current is the ______ where electrical energy is converted into heat energy when current flows through a conductor.
Fill in the blank: Begin with a real-world observation: when you touch a phone ______ after it has been plugged in for a while, it feels warm.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can derive the heat produced in a circuit using H = I²Rt when given current, resistance, and time, and can explain why the heat depends on the square of the current rather than linearly.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Begin with a real-world ______: when you touch a phone charger after it has been plugged in for a while, it feels warm.
